articles.title: Why are sandwiches more regulated than AI?
articles.excerpt: The Bottom LineFuturist Max Tegmark wonders why sandwiches are more regulated than artificial intelligence in the US.The biggest danger facing mankind is a machine that can “outsmart the whole species”, argues Max Tegmark, professor of physics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and founder of the Future of Life Institute.Tegmark tells host Steve Clemons that governments and tech companies are in a “race to replace” human labour, instead of solving human problems. “It’s aimed at getting more money and power to a very small number of individuals,” he says.But a slew of suicides and murders committed by people chatting with AI chatbots has led to pushback against the Silicon Valley “don’t regulate us” lobby.Published On 16 Aug 2026

articles.title: ‘Water and salt’: Qusra residents trapped in Israeli settler siege
articles.excerpt: As the blockade enters its second week, Palestinians remain trapped by settlers and soldiers without water or power.As the siege enters its second week, 15 Palestinians, including two children, remain besieged inside three homes in the Ras al-Ain area of Qusra, south of Nablus. Surrounded by armed Israeli settlers and military battalions and convoys, the families are cut off from food, water, and electricity. The United Nations reported that the residents are “trapped inside their homes in a state of terror, unable to attend to their basic needs and without access to water or electricity”.Stripped of humanityThe humanitarian crisis remained acute on Sunday when the Israeli army intercepted a UNICEF convoy attempting to deliver aid to the trapped families. While the entry of two vehicles provided temporary relief regarding food, military forces blocked and expelled a water tanker from the vicinity of the homes, sustaining the severe deprivation of basic resources. The day prior, settlers attacked municipal workers and a bulldozer attempting to repair utility lines. Qusra Mayor Abdel Azim Wadi told Al Jazeera, “We were unable to restore electricity and water to the three besieged homes in the town.”Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Israeli settlers’ siege of Palestinian homes in West Bank enters fourth daylist 2 of 3Israeli forces order families to evacuate homes in Qusralist 3 of 3Huckabee calls Israeli settlers ‘terrorists’: Can US push end Qusra siege?end of listWadi emphasized the severity of the situation, stating, “Humanely, we have often heard about human rights, about children’s rights, and about women’s rights, but today what our families in Jabal Ras al-Ain are experiencing is truly stripped of humanity.”Al Jazeera’s Laith Jaar, reporting from Qusra, witnessed the military’s direct involvement in enforcing the blockade.

articles.title: Cristiano Ronaldo hints at retirement at end of season
articles.excerpt: Superstar forward gave his clearest indication yet that he could end his playing career after the current season.Cristiano Ronaldo ‌‌has fuelled speculation about his retirement plans after saying ⁠⁠the upcoming ⁠⁠year will probably be the last of his playing career.The 41-year-old Portugal captain is one of the ⁠⁠most decorated players of all time, winning major trophies with Manchester United, Real Madrid, Juventus and current club ⁠⁠Al-Nassr since making his senior debut for Sporting in 2002.Recommended Stories list of 4 itemslist 1 of 4Arsenal trounce Manchester City 3-0 in Community Shield masterclasslist 2 of 4Arsenal defend title against revamped challengers as Premier League returnslist 3 of 4Mohamed Salah’s Trabzonspor debut ends in draw with Kasimpasalist 4 of 4Islam Makhachev wins record 17th straight fight at UFC 330end of listThe five-time Ballon d’Or winner was unable to add a World Cup title to his list of honours after Portugal fell ‌‌short at this year’s tournament, leaving the sport’s biggest prize absent from his trophy cabinet.“This is probably my last year of football and I want to leave a spectacular legacy,” Ronaldo told lifestyle magazine Vogue in an interview published on Sunday.The forward has scored 976 ⁠⁠goals for club and country during a ⁠⁠career spanning more than two decades.“I have so many things to keep me busy that to tell you just one thing is hard. Because ⁠⁠football could leave a big hole, you have to fill your time in various ⁠⁠ways, not just one,” he said.“And ⁠⁠also have more fun, travel more, watch and play padel, which I really like, and continue to enjoy what I’ve earned—what we’ve earned. Because, after ‌‌all, it’s been 25 years with a lot of sacrifice.”Ronaldo will continue playing for Saudi Pro League club Al-Nassr ‌‌this ‌‌season as he closes in on the milestone of 1,000 career goals.

articles.excerpt: The devastating hurricane grazes the Big Island in Hawaii in the US, but avoids making landfall.Hurricane Lala has weakened from a Category 1 hurricane to a tropical storm after passing south of Hawaii, but meteorologists warned that hurricane-force gusts could still batter the islands with punishing winds accompanied by flash flooding.On Saturday, the US National Hurricane Center (NHC) issued a hurricane warning for the Big Island, which has not experienced a direct hurricane landfall in 155 years.Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Storm Lala strengthens into a Category 1 hurricane as it nears Hawaiilist 2 of 3One million evacuated as Typhoon Dolphin pummels east China: What we knowlist 3 of 3Typhoon Dolphin hits eastern China, more than one million evacuatedend of listBut as tropical storm winds swept west from Maui to Oahu and Kauai on Sunday, Hurricane Lala drifted past, edging the Hawaiian coast and just avoiding primary impact zones.Still, pounding waves crashed against the shore of the Big Island. Wild squalls bent tall palm trees and fierce sideways rain swelled rivers.Up to one metre (three feet) of rain was expected on higher windward slopes. Such a torrent could turn rivers into turbulent floods and cause life-threatening mudslides. The NHC said in an advisory published early on Sunday morning that rainfall totals could even reach up to 90cm (35 inches) in some areas of the Big Island.Almost 130,000 utility customers lost power, Reuters reported. Hawaiian Electric warned customers on Saturday evening that hurricane-force winds and rain hampered repair efforts, citing flooded roadways and downed trees. Three hospitals had already switched to generator power, Hawaii’s Governor Josh Green said.At least one person died in a car accident in the South Point area of the Big Island, while 19 roofs were lost in the “enormous storm”.

articles.title: Indonesia Is the Latest Country to Validate China’s Claim to Taiwan – Unwittingly or Not
articles.excerpt: On the morning of August 12, China’s People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) and an Indonesian Navy warship conducted a joint navigation exercise in the waters east of Taiwan. It was the first time China had exercised with a foreign military in these geopolitically sensitive waters. The announcement a day earlier had drawn a swift rebuke from Taiwan’s authorities, which called the exercise an act of political manipulation, “aimed at creating a false impression before the international community that the Chinese communists have jurisdiction over waters east of Taiwan.” The United States similarly called on China “to cease its continuous military pressure against Taiwan.” Chinese state media indeed framed the exercises as evidence of its jurisdiction over the area. The Global Times, a mouthpiece for the Chinese Communist Party, quoted Chinese military affairs expert Zhang Junshe describing the exercise as being of “great significance,” both because it was the first of its kind and because it demonstrated “China’s sovereign rights and jurisdiction over the exclusive economic zone east of Taiwan island.” The exercise came at a moment when Beijing has increased its operational presence in the waters east of Taiwan in an effort to assert its jurisdiction. After Japan and the Philippines agreed to start delimitation talks over their exclusive economic zones (EEZs), which overlap to the east of Taiwan, China sent Coast Guard and law enforcement vessels to patrol the disputed waters in early June. Although the PLAN has regularly held exercises in these waters, it marked the first time the Coast Guard patrolled the region independently. The Coast Guard presence, accompanied by law enforcement and research vessels, were framed as a routine expression of Beijing’s sovereignty over the area. Although initially a special operation, it has now become semi-permanent. And now China is roping in third countries to corroborate its jurisdiction, with state media making this link directly.

articles.title: Singapore’s Israel Tightrope
articles.excerpt: When Singapore gained independence in 1965, it had no army, few resources, and limited room for error. Other countries turned down its requests for military assistance. Israel did not. That history still has relevance as Singapore’s leaders have repeatedly recognized the contribution Israel made at a time when its existence was in jeopardy. Over the decades, the relationship expanded from the original defense collaboration to a broader relationship in technology, cybersecurity, research and the life sciences. In 2025, however, Singapore took an unprecedented step: four Israelis faced financial sanctions and travel bans for “egregious acts of extremist violence” against Palestinians in the West Bank, according to the Foreign Ministry. That decision did not amount to a rupture with Israel, nor did it wipe away the historical appreciation that’s always been a factor in the relationship. Instead, Singapore is communicating that friendship is not synonymous with remaining silent when Israeli actions are at odds with Singapore’s expressed positions on international law and a two-state solution. Following Singapore’s independence from Malaysia in 1965, the government of Lee Kuan Yew sought assistance from several nations in the development of its military. Israel responded by surveying the island with its advisers and structuring a master plan for building up the Singapore Armed Forces from scratch, namely the “Brown Book.” Singapore’s national service system was also heavily inspired by the Israeli model. This assistance was crucial to the fledgling city-state, as it came at a time when Singapore was at existential risk. However, for decades, Singapore’s relationship with Israel was a tightly guarded secret. Overt defense cooperation with Israel was a sensitive subject in Southeast Asia, especially the Muslim world, and Singapore knew that such a move could cause tensions with its neighbors.

articles.title: Taiwan Wants to Know Why Indonesia Joined China in a Naval Exercise East of Taiwan
articles.excerpt: In a rare moment of diplomatic friction, Taiwan has called on the Indonesian government to clarify joint naval exercises with China that took place in waters east of Taiwan. The exercise took place on the morning of August 12, between 6:30 a.m. and 9:30 a.m. As part of the naval exercise, the Indonesian Navy frigate KRI I Gusti Ngurah Rai and the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Navy’s Honghe, a guided-missile frigate under the Eastern Theater Command, practiced maritime maneuvers. The drill included practicing formation, maritime communications, as well as replenishment-at-sea, and concluded with a divergence ceremony. For its part, the Indonesian government has denied that the exercise was threatening in any way. “The passing exercises are not war-fighting in nature, but rather a universal naval tradition conducted when passing through the waters of another country,” the Indonesian Navy said in a statement. It described passex activities in general – including, presumably, the one on August 12 – as “goodwill engagements that are commonly conducted by navies around the world as an expression of naval brotherhood and the maritime diplomacy associated with warships.” Similarly, the Chinese government claimed that the exercises were in the interests of “jointly safeguarding regional peace and stability.” Certainly, the scale of the exercise is not to be overstated, as it only involved two vessels. At the same time, according to geointelligence firm ingeniSPACE in a report published by Domino Theory, the exercise took place in Taiwan’s exclusive economic zone (EEZ). The Indonesian vessel, which had its Automatic Identification System (AIS) on, first entered Taiwan’s EEZ before aligning with the Honghe, which did not have its AIS on – as is common for Chinese vessels operating in Taiwan’s EEZ. The Indonesian frigate later passed close to but did not enter Taiwan’s contiguous zone.

articles.title: Why India Needs a Comprehensive Polar Strategy
articles.excerpt: For generations, India’s strategic policies have been anchored by two geographical features: the Himalayas guarding its northern boundaries and the Indian Ocean protecting its maritime boundaries. However, amid renewed scientific and strategic attention as well as great power competitions, other frontiers – the Arctic Sea and the Antarctic – are quietly redefining the country’s security, economic, and diplomatic landscape. Against this background, the Parliamentary Standing Committee on External Affairs’ report on “India’s Role and Presence in the Arctic and Antarctic Regions” is more than a routine parliamentary exercise. The committee deemed India’s current approach to the polar region inadequate. It recommended appointing a polar ambassador and creating a dedicated Polar Affairs Desk within the Ministry of External Affairs to strengthen capability and pursue a more proactive diplomatic role in both poles. While the recommendation deserves support, appointing a dedicated ambassador should be seen only as a beginning for India’s polar presence. What New Delhi requires is a comprehensive polar strategy that integrates scientific research with diplomacy, maritime interests, climate security, economic needs, and long-term strategic planning. Why the Poles Matter India is not a newcomer to the polar regions. It launched the Indian Antarctic Program in 1981 and established a sustained scientific presence through research stations like Dakshin Gangotri (now decommissioned), Maitri, Bharti, and Maitri II (upcoming). In the Arctic, India’s engagement evolved through the establishment of the Himadri research station in Svalbard (2008), then observer status in the Arctic Council (2012), and finally the adoption of India’s Arctic policy in 2022. While these initiatives have earned India considerable scientific credibility, they also exposed a strategic paradox.

articles.title: In Interview, Japarov Says He’d Planned for Tashiev to Be Kyrgyz President Next
articles.excerpt: Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov claimed in an August 13 interview with journalist Ali Toktakunov that he’d planned for his former ally and security chief Kamshubek Tashiev to follow him in the presidency, but changed course once he realized “he’s not ready.” The revelation comes in tandem with Kyrgyzstan’s prosecutor general appealing the July verdict and sentences in the “Letter of 75” case, seeking harsher punishments. Japarov also clarified in the interview that he will, indeed, seek a second term in January in order to “complete” his reforms. Tashiev served as the head of the State Committee for National Security (SCNS) until his surprising dismissal in February. At the time, Japarov explained the dismissal of his friend and close ally as necessary to “strengthen the unity of the state and prevent divisions in society, including between government agencies.” A month before his dismissal, Tashiev had responded to mounting rumors that he would seek the presidency. “Many have tried and continue to try to sow discord between us, claiming that I aspire to the presidency. But this is not true,” he said at the time. “I do not intend to overthrow Sadyr Nurgoyevich h [Japarov]… In this life, only death can separate us.” Tahsiev has consistently denied any ambition to become president, even as he built up a resume of successes and consolidated power around himself. But Japarov just said he intended to retire after his first term and pass the presidency on to Tashiev. So what happened? According to Japarov, he’d told Tashiev, “Be prepared, cleanse your circle, educate your people.” Tashiev apparently did not do so. “Then I see: he’s not ready,” Japarov continued. “His staff isn’t behaving as expected, and people in his entourage have skyrocketed in power.” When the “Letter of 75” appeared, Japarov said, “When parliament began to be divided between the general’s supporters, I summoned him and said: ‘This is unacceptable. You can’t divide the people.

articles.title: China Forced Nepal to Cancel an International Conference on Tibetan Studies
articles.excerpt: The 17th Seminar of the International Association for Tibetan Studies (IATS) Conference, scheduled to be held at Kathmandu University, Nepal, from August 23-29, was cancelled on August 5 and later shifted online. The cancellation was done by the organizers, at the formal request of the Nepali government. The IATS conference is one of the premier academic forums for Tibetan culture, history, language and religion. The conference was set to bring together scholars from 40 countries, including India, China, and the United States – many of whom had already arranged and paid for costs to attend the conference in Kathmandu. The conference had been in planning for four years, as Nepal was selected to host the seminar in 2022. The abrupt cancellation of the conference on grounds of “security concerns” highlights both Beijing’s ironclad grip and bid to assert authority over Tibetan Buddhism. The cancellation came after Chinese officials expressed concerns over pro-Tibet activists using the platform for demonstrations. Notably, Nepal’s security agencies had ruled out the possibility of a security threat to the event. The pressure came not only from Chinese diplomats but, most remarkably, a religious figure. The Venerable Master Yinshun, former vice president of the Buddhist Association of China and a member of the National Committee of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC) and abbot of the Chinese Temple of Nepal, visited Nepal on July 29. Following his visit, combined with diplomatic efforts by Chinese Ambassador to Nepal Zhang Maoming, around a dozen scholars from the Tibetan Policy Institute in India withdrew their participation from the conference. The cancellation of the conference is consistent with Beijing’s recent efforts to exert control over Nepal’s association with Tibetan Buddhism. This is seen in several pre-emptive and proactive measures taken by Beijing to curb Tibetan Buddhism’s influence in Nepal.

articles.title: In Afghanistan, Growing Resistance Meets Fears of Pakistani Influence
articles.excerpt: August 15 marks five years since the Taliban returned to power, and throughout that time, the group has presented Afghanistan as a country completely under its control. The small armed opposition in Panjshir, Badakhshan, and Baghlan’s Andarab district has not managed to contest the Taliban’s dominance successfully. But the emergence of new anti-Taliban movements across the country has begun to challenge that image. Last month, a new resistance group called Sipahiyan-i-Mihan, or “Soldiers of the Homeland,” briefly captured the center of Yaftal-e Payeen district in Badakhshan. Local sources said its fighters entered the district headquarters, disarmed Taliban personnel, and raised their flag. The group withdrew several hours later and said the withdrawal was voluntary, although the Taliban said the fighters fled when reinforcements arrived. What neither side could deny was that, for the first time since August 2021, a district center had fallen out of Taliban control. The Taliban later sent reinforcements and prepared a larger operation, but so far, no decisive operation against Sipahiyan-i-Mihan has been publicly reported. Other new groups have announced operations as well. This week, the Republic Front of Afghanistan said it had targeted a vehicle carrying the Taliban intelligence chief for Kabul’s 18th district and claimed that he and his companions were killed. Local sources confirmed an explosion, but the casualties remain unverified. The U.S.-based Afghanistan United Front, led by former Afghan army commander General Sami Sadat, also announced “Operation Muharib” and claimed attacks in Kandahar, Helmand, and Badghis. Meanwhile, the established National Resistance Front, led by Ahmad Massoud, son of the legendary anti-Taliban commander Ahmad Shah Massoud, and the Afghanistan Freedom Front, led by former army chief General Yasin Zia, have continued and expanded their struggle.

articles.title: 5 Years After the Fall: Why the World Still Misreads the Taliban
articles.excerpt: Five years have passed since the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan. During this period, the international community tried a wide range of policies to influence the Taliban’s behavior, from humanitarian assistance and political and economic pressure to diplomatic engagement and negotiations that began through indirect channels and, today, in some cases, have developed into direct talks. At the same time, human rights defenders, political opponents of the Taliban, and many ordinary Afghans did not abandon their resistance. From street protests and underground schools to human rights campaigns and various forms of civil disobedience, they sought to prevent the normalization of Taliban rule both within Afghanistan and internationally. Yet neither the international community’s main expectations nor the hopes of many Afghans were realized. An inclusive government did not emerge, political and social restrictions continued, and rather than becoming more flexible, the Taliban further consolidated their system of rule based on their own ideological interpretation of religion. Women were excluded from education, universities, employment, and much of public life, while civic space and fundamental rights came under even tighter restrictions. The most common response to this reality has been to conclude: “The Taliban never changed.” But that answer leaves a more important question unresolved. Why were so many international policies based, from the outset, on the assumption that the Taliban would change? Why did a world that had invested two decades in state-building, modern governance, and rule-based institutions in Afghanistan continue to believe that engagement, economic pressure, or the promise of international legitimacy could change the group’s behavior? Perhaps the central problem was never simply that the Taliban failed to change.

articles.title: Mecca Joint Deterrence Agreement: Implications for India
articles.excerpt: On August 7, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye concluded the Mecca Joint Deterrence Agreement to strengthen “collective deterrence” against any act of aggression. The agreement states that an armed attack against “any one of the three states shall be regarded as an attack against them all.” Signed in the holy city of Mecca by Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, the pact expands the bilateral Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement (SMDA) between Riyadh and Islamabad signed in September 2025, to include Turkiye. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said more countries could join, potentially Egypt, though Cairo hasn’t responded. As per reports, Saudi Arabia has opposed Egypt’s inclusion due to President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi’s growing proximity with the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Drawing a parallel to NATO’s Article 5 that calls for mutual defense, Fidan said the three signatories to the Mecca Agreement would decide through consultations the degree, form, and format of ​support they would request in the event of an attack. The pact has raised several questions on its implications for India. While caution is advised, it shouldn’t be exaggerated for a variety of reasons. Diversifying Security The joint statement issued after the signing of the pact said that it was based on the enduring bonds of “brotherhood and Islamic solidarity” that unite the three countries and builds upon their “shared” strategic interests and longstanding defense cooperation, reflects their “shared commitment” to further strengthening “collective security” and to promoting peace, security, and stability in the “region and beyond,” in pursuit of a secure and prosperous future. Fundamentally, the pact reflects the changing dynamics in the region and the decreasing confidence of West Asian countries in the U.S.

articles.title: Afghanistan: 5 Years in the Dark
articles.excerpt: The Pulse | Society How the Taliban turned Afghanistan into a country where half the population has been ordered to disappear. Credit: X/UN Women Afghanistan Fatima keeps her medical textbooks in a cupboard she no longer opens. Her university ID card, with its photograph of a 19-year-old who intended to become a doctor, sits among them like a relic from another country. In a sense, it is. The Afghanistan that printed the card – a state with a constitution, a free press and women in its universities, courtrooms, and newsrooms – no longer exists. “Sometimes I look at a bird and feel jealous, because it has more freedom than I do,” she told me from Kabul, where, at 24, she describes herself as a prisoner in her own home. “I often think that if the Taliban had not come, I would still be at university, working toward my biggest dream of becoming a doctor. Now, instead of dreaming about my future, I spend my days wondering how I will survive and asking myself, ‘Why me?’” August 15 marks five years since the fall of Kabul, and Fatima’s question has an answer, though not one that offers her any comfort. It is not just her. Roughly 20 million Afghan women and girls have been erased from public life – not by accident or by the chaos of war but by design. Decree by decree, ministry circular by ministry circular, the removal of half of Afghanistan’s population from its schools, offices, parks, and airwaves transitioned seamlessly from an emergency into an administrative routine. A System Built Decree by Decree What began in the autumn of 2021 as a scattering of individual prohibitions has hardened into a legal and bureaucratic machine. According to U.N. monitoring, the Taliban have issued hundreds of decrees and directives since seizing power, a large share of them aimed specifically at women and girls. Each one has shrunk the space in which a woman may learn, work, travel, speak, or simply exist, and together they form what U.N.

articles.title: Restrictions on Foreign Fund Flow to Christian Organizations in India Complicate India-US Ties
articles.excerpt: On March 25, the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment (FCRA) Bill, 2026, was introduced in the Lok Sabha, the lower house of the Indian Parliament. The bill seeks to amend the FCRA Act 2010, which regulates the receipt and use of foreign contributions by individuals and organizations in India. Since 2010, the act has been amended three times, most recently in 2020. A key provision of the recent amendment bill relates to the creation of a “designated authority” under the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), which has been empowered to provisionally take over, manage, and dispose of the assets of an organization if its FCRA registration is canceled, surrendered, or undergoes “deemed cessation” due to non-renewal. This change has generated considerable criticism. On August 12, parliament adopted a motion referring the bill to a 31-member joint parliamentary committee, which will scrutinize the bill and submit its report in the first week of the parliament’s winter session. Beyond strong domestic criticism, especially from opposition parties, the bill has triggered a strong reaction from several American politicians, including Congressman Riley Moore, who slammed the bill as an “attack on Christians.” Senator James Risch, who heads the U.S. Senate Foreign Relations Committee, described the proposed amendments as “deeply concerning” and said the U.S. would not “hesitate to call out countries who violate… human rights of Christians and other religious groups around the world.” In an opinion piece for the Washington Examiner in May, Congressman Chris Smith described the legislation as “designed to set up the expropriation of Indian Christians.” Categorically rejecting such claims, India’s Ministry of External Affairs described the FCRA Amendment Bill as an “internal matter.” In a bid to alleviate Washington’s concerns, India’s Ambassador to the U.S. Vinay Mohan Kwatra took to social media to “debunk” certain “myths” surrounding the proposed bill.

articles.title: The Key Takeaways From the Vietnamese President’s Visit to Australia
articles.excerpt: Vietnam and Australia released three joint statements at the conclusion of Vietnamese President To Lam’s state visit to Australia from August 9-12. The number and significance of these documents show that the two sides did more than exchange pleasantries, offering a clear indication of the upward trajectory in Vietnam-Australia relations. The headline achievement of Lam’s visit was the signing of three separate joint statements: one on deepening the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership (CSP), one on economic resilience cooperation, and one on the enhancement of science, technology, and innovation connectivity. This is unprecedented; no previous visit by either country’s leader has produced three parallel statements. The first statement is essentially political. It reaffirms the strategic trust built between the two nations over five decades and “the strength of the Viet Nam-Australia Comprehensive Strategic Partnership” that the two sides established in March 2024. President Lam and Prime Minister Albanese saw this as a reflection of “the increasing convergence of strategic interests and agreed that cooperation should be ambitious and forward-looking.”\ The second and third statements, by contrast, are more functional and forward-looking. That two of the three statements are devoted to economic resilience and technological cooperation reflects the priorities of the Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV) and the Vietnamese government, which are pushing toward their stated goal of becoming a developed, high-income nation by 2045. They also signal a new shared driver of the bilateral relationship at a moment when global supply chains and technological competition are being reshaped by geopolitical volatility. Perhaps the most striking language in the outcomes refers to the imperative of economic resilience.

articles.title: Indonesia’s Transgender Community Is Facing Growing Repression
articles.excerpt: In October 2025, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto issued a presidential decree outlining the country’s national defense policy and the nonmilitary threats his administration identified as important to the nation’s security. Listed in the latter category, alongside terrorism, radicalism, and drug addiction, was “the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture,” as reported in the Jakarta Post. While the decree drew concern from civil society organizations in Indonesia, particularly pro-democracy and queer rights groups, it initially received limited attention outside Indonesia. Last month, however, a wave of hate crimes targeted transgender women across the country, highlighting Prabowo’s decree and what activists have described as the worsening conditions for LGBTQ+ people in Indonesia. Several transphobic incidents took place during July 14-16 of this year, all of which involved mobs attacking trans women specifically. In one particular instance in the West Java city of Bogor, over 15 trans women were doused with urine, forced to strip naked, and physically beaten in an incident that was recorded and later shared to social media. The online footage itself attracted more hate from some Indonesian netizens, who used slurs and called for further such attacks against trans people. While Indonesia lacks explicitly anti-LGBTQ+ laws, several legal frameworks still indirectly discriminate against queer people, and stigma remains prevalent, largely as a result of conservative Muslim forces in the country. Transgender individuals are permitted to change their legal gender only if they have undergone sex reassignment surgery and subsequently received judicial approval. Same-sex sexual activities, meanwhile, can be criminalized under moral laws. The westernmost province of Aceh, the one Indonesian region governed by syariah law, stands as the most conservative on the issue, punishing homosexual acts with flogging, fines, or even jail time.

articles.title: Thailand Denies Reports It Planned to Use Security Cooperation as US Tariff Leverage
articles.excerpt: The Thai government has denied reports that it plans to use military and security cooperation as leverage in its ongoing trade negotiations with the United States, reaffirming its commitment to the nations’ longstanding security relationship. Rachada Dhanadirek, a spokesperson for the government, said on Wednesday that the talks would focus solely on how to attain fair and balanced trade between the two allies, Thai PBS reported. Her comments came a day after a Bloomberg report stating that Thailand was preparing to warn the Trump administration that steep U.S. tariffs could force it to scale back military cooperation. This included the annual Cobra Gold joint exercises, a cornerstone of the U.S.-Thai alliance that have taken place since 1982. The report quoted an unnamed Thai official familiar with the matter, who said this position was expected to form part of Thailand’s negotiating position in the reciprocal trade negotiations that are set to resume later this month. “While the provision will be broadly worded,” the article stated, “Thailand could reconsider its participation in joint military activities if higher tariffs inflict significant economic damage.” Rachada said yesterday that security cooperation would be quarantined from ongoing U.S. tariff negotiations and would not be used as leverage in the talks. She also said that existing military exchanges will proceed as planned, including Cobra Gold, the last iteration of which in February and March involved about 8,000 personnel from 30 countries. “Thailand and the United States share broad and deep ties across many areas, including the economy, trade, security and people-to-people relations,” Rachada told the press. “Each area has its own framework and national interests that must be carefully considered. The government will not trade one national interest for another.” Thailand has been negotiating a “reciprocal” trade deal with the U.S.

articles.title: Former Myanmar Ambassador to UK Goes on Trial For ‘Trespassing’ in Diplomatic Residence
articles.excerpt: Myanmar’s former ambassador to the United Kingdom appeared in a London court on Wednesday on trespassing charges for refusing to leave a diplomatic residence after being locked out of the embassy. When the military seized power in a coup in February 2021, Ambassador Kyaw Zwar Minn denounced the takeover and pledged his loyalty to the opposition movement. He was immediately dismissed by the junta and locked out of the embassy, but refused to leave Myanmar House, the ambassador’s official residence in northwest London. Kyaw Zwar Minn, now 68, has argued that Myanmar’s military government, which handed power to a “civilian” government in April of this year, was illegitimate and had no authority to ask him to vacate the property. In May of last year, he was charged by London police last week with trespassing on a diplomatic premises between May 2021 and November 2024. During the hearing at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday, Prosecutor Louise Oakley argued that he had been recalled as ​ambassador shortly after the 2021 coup, Reuters reported. She added that the military administration had ⁠instructed Kyaw Zwar Minn to “hand over state-owned properties” by the middle of April 2021, and that Britain’s Foreign Office has also told him to leave the residence. “Having been granted permission to reside at Myanmar House as the ambassador, his refusal to vacate the diplomatic premises after he was removed ​from that position means that ​he is guilty ⁠of the offense of diplomatic trespass,” Oakley said.

articles.title: How Indonesia Can Get Ahead in the Artificial Intelligence Race
articles.excerpt: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming economies around the world, but much of the discussion about it focuses on software, algorithms, computing power, regulation, and talent. While these factors are important, they overlook the one major precondition upon which everything else depends: a reliable supply of electricity. Every AI application ultimately runs inside an AI data center and requires industrial land, electrical substations, cooling systems, fiber-optic connectivity, backup power, and, depending on the cooling technology employed, significant quantities of water. Without this infrastructure and the energy to power it, even the most advanced AI software, algorithms, and talent cannot be deployed at scale. For Indonesia, this raises an important strategic question: Does it have the land, infrastructure, and energy needed to become a leading destination for AI investment? The answer will help determine whether Indonesia becomes a regional AI hub or watches investment flow elsewhere. The Energy Bottleneck in Digital Infrastructure AI is rapidly becoming as dependent on energy as it is on technology. Training advanced AI models requires vast numbers of specialized processors operating continuously for weeks or months. Even after models have been trained, serving millions of AI queries each day creates a permanent and growing demand for electricity. The newest AI data centers already consume hundreds of megawatts of power, while some planned facilities are expected to consume as much electricity as medium-sized cities. In this regard, Indonesia possesses several important advantages. It has Southeast Asia’s largest economy, a population approaching 300 million people, a rapidly expanding digital economy, growing cloud adoption, and government policies that recognize AI as a national priority.

articles.title: How Could the Rise of Progressive Democrats Impact US China Policy?
articles.excerpt: From Analilia Mejia to Abdul El-Sayed to Peggy Flanagan, a progressive winning streak in Democratic primaries has swept across the country in the lead-up to this year’s midterm elections. Unlike most midterm election cycles, where domestic issues dominate the political agenda, foreign policy has been thrust into the spotlight this time, with the Israel-Palestine conflict emerging as the defining litmus test of the Democratic Party. As progressive candidates have rallied behind the Palestinian cause in their battles against AIPAC-backed moderates, the party’s leftward ideological shift could impact not only the decades-long Israel-U.S. alliance, but also Washington’s policy toward its greatest strategic competitor: China. Progressives perceive the world through the lens of structural inequality. That worldview lies at the heart of their dissatisfaction with the status quo of the U.S. socioeconomic structure: a widening gap between economic elites and ordinary people. As a result, they fight against corporate interests and political corruption, thereby translating their opposition to economic elites into opposition to the political establishment. The same logic applies to foreign affairs – progressives can readily translate their anti-establishment sentiment into opposition to American primacy, which has long been buttressed by bipartisan support for U.S. military dominance. This helps explain why Palestine has become such a powerful cause on the left. Progressives tend to view U.S.-backed Israel as an extension of American power in the Middle East and Palestinians as victims of U.S. hegemony. Hence, although a parallel anti-Israel sentiment can also be seen among some Republicans, progressive Democrats have a fundamentally different motivation for their opposition to Israel.

articles.title: Why Is Everyone Playing Mahjong?
articles.excerpt: Mahjong is having a global moment. From designer tile sets and “mahjong parties” to growing numbers of clubs and classes, the centuries-old Chinese tile game is becoming trendy once again. But its resurgence raises questions about cultural exchange, commercialization, and what happens when a tradition rooted in Chinese history becomes a “lifestyle trend.” Mahjong emerged in eastern coastal China in the mid 1800s, towards the end of the Qing Dynasty. Although its exact origins are debated, historians agree the game developed from earlier Chinese tile-based games. In the early 1900s, mahjong spread across China and internationally, including to the United States, France and the United Kingdom. Annelise Heinz, historian of modern America, explained how American businesses marketed the game as an exotic Chinese novelty, often using Orientalist imagery in related advertisements and media. American companies such as Abercrombie & Fitch helped commercialize mahjong. But Heinz argued that their success depended on Chinese manufacturing, commercial networks, and cultural expertise. Chinese merchants and community members imported and sold mahjong sets, and taught many White Americans how to play – yet their contributions are often overlooked. Mahjong traditionally involves four players drawing and discarding from 144 tiles to create winning combinations. Strategy, probability, memory, and your ability to read your opponents all play a role. The social experience is also equally important. Today, there are more than 40 iterations of mahjong played globally, with different versions having different rules and varying numbers of players and tiles. Chinese variants such as the Cantonese and Hong Kong styles differ from other versions such as Japanese riichi mahjong. One of the most distinctive adaptations is American Mah Jongg. Developed in the 1920s, this version has its own rules, and a number of joker tiles that don’t exist in the original version.

articles.title: Can South Korea’s $880 Billion AI Ambition Help Cement Its Status as a High-Tech Powerhouse?
articles.excerpt: Much has been made of the artificial intelligence race between the United States and China, but it’s South Korea that’s currently making significant headway in its ambitious AI buildout. In June, President Lee Jae-myung announced plans for at least $880 billion of investments to build out the country’s chip manufacturing and artificial intelligence capabilities over the years ahead. The plans come as part of the country’s Three Mega Projects to develop new chip production hubs domestically, as well as data centers and robotics technology. While the investment is also focused on boosting the economies of areas outside of Seoul, Lee pointedly claimed that South Korea must outpace regional rivals like China, Taiwan, and Japan, all of whom are investing heavily in chip factories and other advanced technologies as part of a widespread AI boom period. South Korea has already emerged as an early AI leader thanks to the whirlwind success of its chipmakers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, both of which currently make up the lion’s share (around 51 percent) of the nation’s total benchmark KOSPI index market capitalization. The rise of South Korea’s artificial intelligence chipmakers has been nothing short of emphatic. At the time of writing, SK Hynix’s five-year growth spurt sits at precisely 1,250 percent, while Samsung’s 205 percent rally over the same period is a wild success for a company that’s already long been established as one of the largest in Asia. But it now appears that plans are firmly underway to ensure that South Korea’s chipmaking strength can help to facilitate a stronger global position when it comes to the AI buildout. But can it really compete with competitors worldwide? South Korea’s AI prowess is far from a secret. Last month, the Bank of America identified South Korea as the strongest overall AI contender over both the short and long term outside of the United States and China.

articles.title: North Korea Fires Ballistic Missiles, Deepening Silence Fuels Analyst Speculation
articles.excerpt: North Korea fired what appeared to be a midrange ballistic missile toward the ocean east of the peninsula on August 12, its second launch in less than a week, according to South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS). The back-to-back launches came two days after South Korea and the United States announced their plans for joint drills. The annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise is set to begin on August 17. The allies describe the drills as defensive. but North Korea has for years denounced them as invasion rehearsals and has frequently responded with weapons tests timed around the training period. The missile lifted off from the Wonsan area on North Korea’s east coast around 6 a.m. and flew more than 700 kilometers, or about 435 miles, before falling into the sea. Authorities in South Korea, the United States, and Japan tracked the launch from its early stages and were still analyzing its exact specifications as of this writing. The JCS did not disclose the missile’s type or flight angle, a departure from its usual practice of offering at least a preliminary classification within hours of a launch. By South Korea’s count, it was Pyongyang’s 11th ballistic missile launch of 2026. The test followed a shorter-range ballistic missile that North Korea fired from the same Wonsan area on August 6. That earlier test was Pyongyang’s first ballistic weapons test in 48 days, breaking a lull that had persisted since its missile launch on June 25. Kim Jong Un, the autocratic leader of North Korea, was shown new missile systems that day, including a modular launcher developed as an analogue of the U.S. HIMARS rocket system. South Korea’s presidential national security office convened emergency meetings after both launches, calling them provocations that violate United Nations Security Council resolutions and urging Pyongyang to halt such tests immediately.

articles.title: The US Military Can’t Function Without China
articles.excerpt: The manufacture of modern weapons begins with complex materials, especially those containing rare earth elements. These elements are used to make everything from magnets and sensors to radars and lasers. According to the U.S. Department of Defense, an F-35 fighter requires more than 400 kilograms of rare earths to build; a destroyer and submarine, respectively, can require anywhere from two to five metric tons. Rare earths also appear in Tomahawk missiles, Predator drones, and the many missiles and bombs that have been used in Iran over the last few months. The problem for the U.S. military is that China accounts for roughly 70 percent of all rare earth mining and more than 90 percent of all rare earth processing, dominating entire categories of critical materials needed to make semiconductors, avionics, batteries, and things that go boom. According to the U.S. Geological Survey, China leads global production in 30 of 44 critical minerals while maintaining, in each of those 30 minerals, at least one monopoly in mining, refining, or processing. Of the many components employed in modern military manufacturing, rare earth magnets are among the most important. Neodymium magnets are prized for being able to produce enormous magnetic forces relative to their low mass, making them invaluable for motors and guidance systems, where every bit of additional weight or electricity consumption can bring debilitating inefficiencies. Supplementing with other rare earths like dysprosium or terbium can make these magnets retain performance at high temperatures while adding samarium and cobalt can enhance stability under pressure, especially useful when flying things at high velocities. In 2025, China mined an estimated 270,000 metric tons of these elements out of a global total of 390,000 tons, accounting for roughly 69 percent of the world’s extraction. Samarium is probably one of the most important rare earths you have never heard of.

articles.title: Can Japan’s Defense Industry Meet its Ambitious Goals?
articles.excerpt: MHI launched Tatsuta, the eleventh Mogami-class frigate on order for the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force, in a ceremony held at its facilities in Nagasaki, Japan, July 2, 2025. Credit: Takahashi Kosuke On August 4, the Japanese Ministry of Defense published its annual 2026 Defense White Paper, which outlines Japan’s defense policies and activities. While the report extensively covers the increasingly severe security environment surrounding Japan, notable highlights include an emphasis on one of Japan’s core concepts, “new ways of defense,” and its defense production. Notably, the White Paper follows Japanese Defense Minister Koizumi Shinjiro’s comment at the Farnborough International Airshow: “Defense production is deterrence itself. No matter how advanced a defense system may be, it means little if it cannot be produced.” His statement suggests a fundamental shift in how Japan views deterrence: rather than mere possession of defense materiel, Japan increasingly recognizes the importance of the defense industrial base as a source of strategic capability. Japan, like other countries around the world, is learning from Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Some of the takeaways include the decisive role played by unmanned assets, renewed appreciation for strong air defense, and the importance of sustaining a defense industrial base that can keep up with a protracted war. Furthermore, recent conflict in the Middle East and concerns about diminishing U.S. stockpiles have sparked concern among U.S. allies about the reliability of the United States as a supplier of advanced munitions for their militaries. These conflicts have served as critical turning points in Japan’s defense posture, prompting the Japanese government to rethink its defense policies to invest more in developing indigenous capabilities and partner with other U.S. allies that share similar concerns.

articles.title: Competing Interests, Common Narrative: How Industry Shapes the AI Race
articles.excerpt: A recent Wall Street Journal article warned that the “[c]lampdown on top U.S. artificial intelligence is fueling concern that Washington is handing Beijing a cyberwarfare advantage.” It went on to note that China’s release of Z.ai by Zhipu AI is on par with Anthropic’s Mythos model in detecting software vulnerabilities. The article, along with a growing body of recent commentary, taps into the prevailing China-U.S. AI race narrative at a time when the United States is deliberating a unified AI policy and reportedly considering banning Chinese open weight models. The AI race narrative holds that the United States and China are engaged in a zero-sum contest to develop and deploy frontier AI so as to accrue lasting geoeconomic advantage. In a May 2026 article for the Transformer newsletter, Yi-Ling Liu outlined how Silicon Valley’s major companies have themselves pushed this AI race narrative, potentially overstating the extent of the competition. However, the interests of these companies are not uniform, nor are the policies that they advocate. Different firms across the AI value chain have continued to invoke the AI race narrative to advance policy preferences that align with their commercial interests. Given the concentrated nature of the global AI supply chain, a select few companies have immense stakes in how policies and regulations on AI evolve and, consequently, strong incentives to shape them. Sitting atop the hardware segment of the AI supply chain is Nvidia, which accounts for over 80 percent of global AI chip sales. Nvidia’s GPUs form the backbone of the compute infrastructure required to train and develop generative AI models. This market position, while enviable, has exposed Nvidia to the broader geoeconomic disruptions that have emanated from the AI race with China.

articles.title: How the Modi Government is Downgrading India’s National Anthem
articles.excerpt: On August 15, when India celebrates its Independence Day, the official celebrations from the ramparts of the Red Fort in New Delhi will, for the first time in 80 years, mark a departure from tradition. India’s national anthem “Jana Gana Mana” (The Minds of All People), which was penned by Nobel laureate Rabindranath Tagore, will be preceded by the singing of the national song, “Vande Mataram” (Hail Mother India) Singing the national song first was a clear move by India’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government to “degrade the national anthem to a secondary status,” The Wire pointed out. This is significant as the national anthem has constitutional status and, as per official protocol, is considered the highest musical symbol of the republic. However, the BJP and its affiliates in the Sangh Parivar have never been fond of the secular content of the national anthem and have consistently demanded primacy for the more controversial Vande Mataram, which has clear Hindu religious overtones. Recently, the Narendra Modi government amended the law to bring Vande Mataram on par with the Jana Gana Mana. Previously, while the national anthem was played on state and ceremonial occasions, the national song was largely restricted to cultural events, and even then it was only its first two verses that were sung. The Defense Ministry, which is in charge of the Independence Day celebrations, announced recently that “in a first,” Vande Mataram would be specially honored to commemorate the song’s 150th anniversary. Per the new protocol, on Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s arrival at the Red Fort, the national song will be played first, the national flag will then be unfurled accompanied by the national anthem. To the uninitiated, this may seem a needless controversy over a non-issue. It is not.

articles.title: Vietnam’s Top Leader Concludes Australia Visit With Trade, Defense in Focus
articles.excerpt: Vietnamese President To Lam’s visit to Australia this week highlighted the burgeoning relationship between the two countries. Given that much of Australia’s large Vietnamese diaspora remains suspicious of the Communist Party of Vietnam – and South Vietnam flags are often seen flying in suburbs with a concentration of Vietnamese Australians – there is a domestic balancing act that the Australian government needs to perform. However, the convergence of interests between the two countries is now proving the stronger pull. The focus of Lam’s visit was on new economic and security agreements. The now dominant lens of Australia’s foreign policy perceives economic security as a central pillar of national security. The economic angle is where the most movement is already happening. Since 2020, two-way trade has doubled, with Vietnam now approaching Australia’s list of top ten trading partners. The specific measures announced this week were mostly incremental: greater agricultural access (including kangaroo meat), and creating smoother services within e-commerce and banking sectors. The low-cost airline Vietjet confirmed it will fly into the new Western Sydney Airport, due to be opened later this year. These are not transformative arrangements, but things that push the relationship forward in important ways. The major development was Vietnam approving a license for the Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT) to open a campus in Hanoi. The university had already established a campus in Ho Chi Minh City in 2000, and has been keen to establish itself as a major driver of the bilateral relationship, including through the creation of the Australia Vietnam Policy Institute to facilitate building the relationship between the two countries. This is part of a broader push by the Australian university sector to embed itself in Southeast Asia, with four other universities operating in Malaysia and Indonesia.

articles.title: Vietnam, Rare Earths, and the Evolving China Plus One Strategy
articles.excerpt: Over the past few years, China Plus One has reshaped global production, helping Vietnam emerge as an important manufacturing base. China Plus One involves companies reducing their excessive dependence on a single production base (i.e., China) by adding capacity elsewhere, which many have already done. However, the next stage of this strategy is likely to be more complicated. Export controls and economic security concerns are exposing vulnerabilities further upstream, particularly in industries that depend on critical minerals. This has demonstrated that even if a company can diversify where it manufactures, it may remain dependent on concentrated supplies of the materials, components, and processing capabilities necessary for that production. Vietnam illustrates this challenge particularly well. China Plus One has brought major investments and increasingly sophisticated manufacturing activities to the country. Amkor Technology, for example, has invested $1.6 billion in a semiconductor assembly, testing, and packaging facility in Bac Ninh province outside Hanoi. Such investments have deepened Vietnam’s links to technologically intensive global supply chains and have made the security of critical inputs increasingly relevant to the country’s economy. Among the most important of these inputs are rare earth elements. China remains dominant across the rare-earth value chain, accounting for more than 90 percent of global refined output and permanent-magnet production, according to the International Energy Agency. China’s export controls have made this dependence more visible, and highlighted how diversifying the location of factories does not necessarily involve the diversification of the supply chains supporting them. A product assembled in Vietnam may still depend on rare-earth materials, magnets, or other critical inputs processed in China.

articles.title: Myanmar’s Resistance Finally Has a Unified Front
articles.excerpt: I was serving as Dean of the University of Medicine in Yangon when Myanmar’s military staged its coup in February 2021. Overnight, I became an activist in the resistance movement, serving in a variety of roles. Like millions of my fellow citizens, I joined peaceful protests and helped lead the Civil Disobedience Movement. My involvement soon made me a wanted man, forcing me to flee to a neighboring country before I eventually received refuge in Europe. I was later appointed minister of health and education in the National Unity Government (NUG), which was formed in April 2021 to lead the resistance to the coup. Since then, throughout what has become known as the Myanmar Spring Revolution, I have witnessed both its triumphs and its setbacks firsthand. Living abroad also allowed me to engage extensively with foreign governments and Myanmar diaspora communities before I returned to Myanmar in 2025. I am now based in one of Myanmar’s liberated areas – territories under the control of revolutionary forces. Against this backdrop, I believe the recent creation of the Steering Council for the Emergence of a Federal Democratic Union (SCEF) represents the most significant turning point in Myanmar’s resistance movement since the 2021 coup. Some have dismissed the SCEF as merely another acronym. Nothing could be further from the truth. It represents one of the most consequential political and military realignments in Myanmar’s modern history. It addresses one of the central weaknesses that has long undermined Myanmar’s democratic struggle: the inability of anti-military forces to sustain a unified political and military front across ethnic and ideological lines.

articles.title: Japan’s Underground Lab Wants to Solve the World’s Nuclear Waste Problem
articles.excerpt: Reindeer pastures and dairy farms stretch across the flat, windswept plain of Japan’s northernmost prefecture, giving little hint of what lies roughly 300 meters below. Inside the Horonobe Underground Research Laboratory, teams of engineers are trying to answer a question no country has fully solved: how to keep highly radioactive waste isolated from the environment for periods measured not in decades, but in tens of thousands of years. In May, I gained special access to the facility through the Japan Atomic Energy Agency (JAEA), touring the underground galleries and observing several of the experiments currently underway. Horonobe Underground Research Laboratory. Photo ©Piergiorgio Pescali. A Rare Laboratory in Sedimentary Rock Horonobe is one of only two underground research laboratories Japan has built to study geological disposal of high-level radioactive waste, and the only one still operating. Its counterpart, the Mizunami Underground Research Laboratory in Gifu Prefecture, was built in crystalline rock and was decommissioned in 2022 after its land lease expired. Horonobe, by contrast, sits in Neogene-era sedimentary rock, giving the JAEA a very different and, officials argue, complementary geological environment to study. The project traces back to November 2000, when the governor of Hokkaido, the mayor of Horonobe town, and the president of the JAEA signed an agreement to permit research on the deep geological environment at the site. Construction and excavation followed over the next two decades, and the laboratory now includes shafts and galleries used to test how engineered barriers, groundwater, and surrounding rock interact over time – the same combination of natural and artificial safeguards that would, in theory, protect a real repository.

articles.title: Data of 15 Million Kazakhstanis Allegedly Leaked
articles.excerpt: Hackers have allegedly posted the personal data of 15 million Kazakhstani citizens for sale on the dark web. If confirmed, this would mark the second major breach of Kazakhstani citizen data in a little over a year. According to RFE/RL, the Mash Telegram channel, which the outlet characterized as linked to the Russian security forces, reported that hackers had put the personal data of 15 million Kazakhstani citizens up for sale on the dark web. The seller reportedly claimed to have obtained the data after hacking Kazakhstan’s eGov service. The file is apparently valued at around $32,000 and, the seller claims, contains passport information, phone numbers, email addresses, document scans, and website passwords. Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development acknowledged the reports and is reviewing them. In a statement posted to Telegram, the ministry said, “At this time, there is no confirmed evidence of a breach of e-government information systems or that the database in question was obtained directly from eGov.” The ministry cited inconsistencies between the claim and the structure of the eGov platform. Data breaches are a fact of modern life the world over. Governments, including Kazakhstan’s, have increasingly pushed to digitalize services. On the one hand, the elimination of physical paperwork and office visits speeds service delivery, eliminating layers of bureaucracy and opportunities for petty corruption. But on the other hand, e-government introduces new risks, can obscure decisionmaking, and provides novel opportunities for corruption and crime. This latest report of leaked citizen data is not the first breach. In June 2025, the SecuriXy.kz Telegram channel reported that an archive containing information on 16.3 million Kazakhstani citizens had been leaked. The files reportedly contained 15.8 million IINs (individual identification numbers), 17 million phone numbers, alongside full names, dates of birth, and addresses.

articles.title: ‘Silence Is Not an Option’: The Quest to Bear Witness to China’s Uyghur Camps
articles.excerpt: “When evil-doing comes like falling rain, nobody calls out ‘stop!’ When crimes begin to pile up they become invisible.” German playwright Bertolt Brecht’s observation on the political apathy that engulfed Germany in the 1930s resonates with 21st century survivors of the Chinese state’s war against Uyghurs in its northwestern heartland, known by exiles as East Turkestan. Germany’s slide into fascism brought book burnings and arrests of “undesirables.” It lead step by step to antisemitism, concentration camps, torture, and death. That brutal history echoes today in Beijing’s campaign against the Turkic peoples of its western regions – and in the silence of a deaf world. Only those who have experienced the terror first-hand and survived to tell the tale can hope to describe its full horrors. Kalbinur Sidik (formerly Romanized as Qelbinur Sidik) is one such rare eyewitness to what many nations have termed a genocide. Her ordeal as a teacher inside the camps drove her to the brink of collapse. She escaped in 2019 ostensibly for medical treatment, hoping to reunite with her daughter in the Netherlands and seek asylum. Speaking out became her path to healing. She told The Diplomat that “silence is not an option.” The faces of captives in her class have haunted her to this day. Since leaving, her mission has been to give voice to their silent cries. Her memoir, “Heart Full of Light” – a title reflecting the meaning of her name, Kalbinur – is full of horror and sadness but also memory, dignity and resistance. It is a cry against erasure and a wake-up call to a world that has not been listening. The book begins with a child immersed in Uyghur culture and belonging, but there was darkness from the start. Sidik grew up cowed by the humiliation of her parents during the Cultural Revolution, a stigma that her family never shook off. Teaching offered hope but the glass ceiling separating her and her colleagues from the dominant Han Chinese was impenetrable.

articles.title: EN DIRECT, guerre en Ukraine : dix-neuf personnes tuées après des frappes de drones et de missiles en Ukraine et en Russie
articles.excerpt: Le ministère de la défense ukrainien affirme avoir « mis hors service 7 des 10 plus grands centres logistiques de l’entreprise d’e-commerce Wildberries ». Live animé par Minh Dréan et Allison Ferrera (service Photo) Après une frappe de missile contre un marché aux livres, à Kiev, le 16 août 2026. GLEB GARANICH/REUTERS Posez votre question à la rédaction : Réagissez Ecrivez votre message ici Votre pseudo... Le 16/08 à 21:00 L’essentiel De nombreuses frappes en Ukraine et en Russie ; Wildberries encore ciblé par l’Ukraine… Ce qu’il faut savoir dimanche 16 août à 21 heures Sept morts en Ukraine au cours de la journée après des frappes russes à Kryvy Rih, Zaporijia, Soumy et Donetsk. Des drones et des missiles russes ont tué deux personnes dans une aciérie d’ArcelorMittal à Kryvy Rih, dans le centre-est de l’Ukraine. Une autre frappe sur Kryvy Rih dans la soirée a fait un mort. Des attaques ont aussi visé d’autres régions, tuant deux personnes dans celle de Zaporijia, une dans celle de Soumy et une autre dans celle de Donetsk. En Russie, douze personnes ont été tuées. une vague de plusieurs centaines de drones ukrainiens a causé la mort de cinq personnes dans une zone résidentielle de la région méridionale de Rostov. Trois autres personnes ont été tuées dans les régions de Belgorod, Koursk et Moscou, et quatre autres dans les territoires ukrainiens sous autorité russe. Le gouverneur de la région de Moscou, Andreï Vorobiov, a qualifié l’attaque d’« une des plus massives de mémoire récente ». Le ministère de la défense ukrainien affirme avoir « mis hors service 7 des 10 plus grands centres logistiques de l’entreprise d’e-commerce Wildberries », à la suite de la frappe qui a touché un centre dans le parc industriel Koledino. Celui-ci était, selon le ministère, « le plus grand centre Wildberries, en superficie ».
